newsitem.title: GERMANY: Protestant church worries over German tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Protestant church worries over German tax cuts.

text.p: Germany's Protestant churches said on Friday that government plans to cut taxes in 1999 could knock one-tenth off the eight billion marks ($4.88 billion) in annual revenues they get in church taxes.

"We face unknown financial demands," Otto von Campenhausen, administrator of the EKD evangelical church movement, said. "We don't know whether regional churches and the EKD will be able to balance their budgets after 1999."

Finance Minister Theo Waigel unveiled proposals on Thursday to slash German income taxes. Registered German Protestants and Catholics pay an income tax surcharge which brings 17 billion marks into church coffers each year.
The church tax is a surcharge of up to nine percent on income taxes -- which under Waigel's tax plan would be slashed by 69 billion marks in 1999.
Church members must pay the surcharge unless they decide officially to leave their church. There are over 50 million registered Catholics and Protestants in Germany. ($1=1.6383 Mark)
